passage: For three years Charu had told friends she "could have" got into the Kolkata repertory company if she'd bothered to audition properly. This year the audition was on the 14th. She printed the monologue, stuck it on the fridge, and rehearsed every evening after work while her flatmate Lavanya timed her. "You're really doing it this time," Lavanya said one night. "Yes." Charu wiped her face with her dupatta. "If I fully prepare and still don't get in, at least I'll know what to work on. That's scarier than not trying. But it's the only way to find out." On the 14th she walked out of the audition hall shaky but smiling. The panel had said her voice was strong, her movement stiff. She wrote "movement class" in her diary that same evening.

qa.a: The panel said her voice was strong and her movement stiff.

qa.a: Lavanya, timing the rehearsals, gets to watch Charu take a real risk, which may feel far more hopeful than three years of maybes.

'You're still up?' Damini asked, finding her brother at the dining table at midnight with index cards everywhere.
'The panel interview is Friday,' Tanvir said. 'Design lead. They'll grill me on the portfolio.'
'Last year you said you'd just "wing it" for the Mumbai one.'
'And then I told everyone I didn't get it because I didn't prepare.' He tapped a card. 'That felt safe. But I learned nothing.'
'So this time?'
'This time I prepare every answer. If I still don't get it, then it's real feedback. It'll hurt. But I'll know where I actually stand.'
Damini pulled a chair closer and picked up the cards. 'Right. Question one. Why should we hire you?'
Tanvir laughed, sat up straighter, and answered.

qa.a: The panel interview on Friday for a design lead role.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir say last year's excuse 'felt safe'?
qa.a: Blaming the lack of preparation meant the rejection didn't touch his ability, but it also meant he learned nothing about where he stood.

qa.q: What choice is Tanvir making this time, and what might it cost him?
qa.a: He is preparing every answer so any result is real feedback; it risks a painful 'no' that he can't explain away.

qa.q: What does Damini's picking up the cards show about how she sees his new approach?
qa.a: Damini seems to respect the change and wants to back it, turning her surprise into practical help at midnight.

grounding: A young man tells his sister he will prepare fully so that any rejection becomes real feedback.

passage: I'm Gurpreet, and for years I entered writing contests with stories finished the night before. When I didn't place, I'd say, "Well, I dashed it off." It was comfortable. This spring I decided to try the city short-story prize properly. I wrote for six weeks, sent drafts to my friend Nirmala, and rewrote the ending three times after her notes. The night before submitting, I sat with my finger over the button, thinking: if this doesn't place, I can't blame the rush. It might just not be good enough yet. I clicked anyway. It didn't win. But the judges' notes said my dialogue was alive and my middle section dragged. For the first time, a result actually told me something. I've started cutting that middle.

qa.q: How many times did Gurpreet rewrite the ending?
qa.a: Gurpreet rewrote the ending three times after Nirmala's notes.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet thinking with a finger over the submit button?
qa.a: Gurpreet was afraid that, with no rush to blame, a loss might simply mean the story wasn't good enough yet.

qa.q: Which choice turned the loss into something useful?
qa.a: Preparing fully meant the judges' notes on the dialogue and the middle section were real information, so Gurpreet could start cutting the middle.

qa.a: Nirmala, who read the drafts, may feel glad to be part of a real attempt and proud that Gurpreet kept going after not winning 🙂.

Teacher's note, Carnatic vocal class, Saturday. Seema.
Leela (24) has decided to audition for the fellowship in December. For two years she has said she 'might, if she has time'. This year she came in with a written plan: forty minutes of practice before work, one recorded mock audition every Sunday, and a list of the three ragas she is weakest in.
Today she told me, 'If I really prepare and still don't get in, at least I'll know what the panel thinks I'm missing. If I half prepare, I learn nothing.' Her voice shook a little on that.
Her first mock recording had shaky gamakas in the slow section. She didn't explain it away. She marked the timestamp and asked for extra time on it.
Next step: I've booked her a mock audition with two outside teachers in October, so the real one isn't the first time strangers judge her.

qa.q: How long does Leela plan to practise before work?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Leela's voice shake when she spoke about not getting in?
qa.a: Full preparation means a rejection would really be about her singing; she is scared of that, yet chooses it because it would tell her something useful.

qa.q: Which of Leela's choices shows she is treating a poor result as information?
qa.a: Marking the timestamp of the shaky gamakas and asking for extra time on it instead of explaining it away; a weak spot becomes something to work on.

qa.q: How might Seema see the change from 'might, if she has time' to a written plan?
qa.a: Seema seems encouraged and takes it seriously, booking an outside mock audition, which suggests trust that Leela is now fully committed.

grounding: A teacher notes a young adult who prepares fully for a risky audition and accepts that a poor result would then be useful information.

Tuesday, 11 p.m.
Six weeks to the women's state trials. Today I did the full session: sprints at six, ball work after office, stretching with Madhuri counting for me. Legs like wet rope.
Old me would have skipped half of this so I could say 'I wasn't really training' if I didn't make it. I did exactly that at nineteen. Never found out if I was good enough. That's worse than a no.
This time I'm doing all of it. If the selectors say no after I've given everything, fine, that's information: maybe my first touch, maybe my speed. I'll know what to fix.
It scares me, though. No hiding spot.
Madhuri said, 'Whatever happens, Vandana, you'll have actually played.' Stuck that on the mirror.
Ice pack, bed.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do during the stretching?
qa.a: Madhuri counted for Vandana.

qa.q: Why does training fully this time scare Vandana?
qa.a: Vandana feels afraid and exposed: with no excuse left, a 'no' from the selectors would really be about her, and there is 'no hiding spot'.

qa.q: What choice sits at the heart of this entry, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Doing every session so that any result means something; a rejection after full effort shows what to fix, while half-training at nineteen taught nothing.

qa.q: How does Madhuri seem to see Vandana's attempt?
qa.a: Madhuri seems proud and supportive, valuing that Vandana will have 'actually played' more than whether the selectors say yes. 🙂

grounding: A young woman chooses to train fully for football trials and accept any result as information, instead of keeping an excuse ready.
